newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Assembly OKs bill to allow smokers' lawsuits.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Assembly OKs bill to allow smokers' lawsuits.

text.p: The California state Assembly passed a bill Thursday to allow individual smokers to sue tobacco companies.
The bill passed 42-19 and was sent back to the state Senate for concurrence in some amendments. The Senate has already passed an earlier version of the bill.
The bill would then require California Gov. Pete Wilson's signature to become law and would not take effect until January.
"It sends a strong message that we can protect the health of the people of California," said Assemblyman Kevin Shelley, a Democrat who backed the bill.

The bill, written by state Sen. Quentin Kopp, an independent, had seemed dead only a week ago when it failed by five votes to achieve the majority needed for passage in the Assembly. But the bill was brought back to the floor for reconsideration Thursday and after a lengthy debate passed.

"I'm pleased that enough members finally came to their senses, because it's illogical, it's unfair to California victims of smoking to preclude them from having an opportunity to present their claims to a jury of their peers," Kopp said.

A 1987 California law exempted tobacco and other "inherently unsafe" products from liability lawsuits. The state legislature passed a limited amendment to the law last month which allowed the state to sue the tobacco industry, which it promptly did. But it said nothing about individuals.
Kopp's bill goes further by removing tobacco from the list of products protected from liability lawsuits, thereby allowing lawsuits by individuals.
Supporters of the bill said it was essential to allow individual Californians to take advantage of the money made available through the proposed federal settlement with the tobacco industry.

The proposed $368.5 billion agreement hammered out by state attorneys general last month would ban future class-action lawsuits over tobacco liability but would still allow smokers to sue individually.
Opponents in the Assembly argued that smokers knew the health risks of smoking and that the bill would just be a boon to trial lawyers.
Kopp said he was optimistic that Wilson, a Republican, would sign the bill.

Steve Tatum, a spokesman for Wilson, said the governor had not yet taken a position on the bill. "We are in the process of looking at the federal settlement and ascertaining how the federal settlement impacts California in particular," Tatum said.
